Bondsmen don't have to post the bond amount - they are vetted and licensed by the state and courts to be responsible for ensuring the appearance and return of bonded defendants. The bondsman may or may not be required to post their own surety bond with the court to be an approved bondsman for that court, but they generally do not post any sort of bond for any particular defendant.

Usually, defendants don't have the liquid assets to post their own bond. It's one of the biggest disconnections in our (in)justice system. Instead, they're expected to find a bondsman and pay them to post a surety bond on their behalf. The fee is usually ten percent of the bail set by the court, and it is non-refundable in all cases. Basically, you have to pay a court-approved company ten percent of your bail if you want to keep your job, see your family, maintain your home, possessions, and effects, etc.

Of course those costs go up if you miss a court date or skip out and the bondsman has to come collect you and bring you in, but that's part of your contract with the bondsman. They are usually (always?) deputized by the court to use necessary private property access, force, and restraint to effect the return of a defendant they have bonded who has skipped.
